about: General design guidance every catalog can include: credentials, forms, accessibility semantics, text, theming and actions. Each rule quotes official Android guidance and links it. A rule's platforms name the catalog platforms (mobile, foundation, wear, glasses, remote-compose) it is carried into; none means every one. Wear catalogs get Wear-specific input and sign-in rules instead of the phone form rules, and Remote Compose catalogs get none of the text-entry rules.

rules.guidance: SecureTextField is a composable built on top of state-based text fields for writing a password field.
rules.check: Judge from the source and the accessibility nodes. Is every field that takes a password, PIN or other secret masked — a SecureTextField / OutlinedSecureTextField, or a text field with PasswordVisualTransformation — rather than a plain text field that shows what is typed? Answer YES when the subject has no such field.

rules.guidance: You can create an icon to hide or show a password based on a user toggle to improve security and enhance the user experience.
rules.check: Does each masked password field offer a show/hide toggle — a trailing icon button, with a content description, that reveals the password on request? Answer YES when the subject has no password field.

rules.guidance: To indicate that a TextField is Autofill-enabled, set the ContentType semantics with the types that the field can accept. This indicates to Autofill services what kind of user data might be relevant to this specific field.
rules.check: Does each field for a username, email address, password, new password or one-time code set its autofill content type (Modifier.semantics { contentType = ContentType.Username / EmailAddress / Password / NewPassword / SmsOtpCode })? The accessibility data does not carry this yet, so decide from the source; if the source is not given, ask for it rather than guessing. Answer YES when the subject has no such field.

rules.guidance: For a one-time password in a single view, you can use AUTOFILL_HINT_SMS_OTP.
rules.check: Is a one-time or verification code field marked as one for autofill (ContentType.SmsOtpCode in Compose, the AUTOFILL_HINT_SMS_OTP hint in Views), so the code can be filled in from the SMS? The accessibility data does not carry this yet, so decide from the source; if the source is not given, ask for it rather than guessing. Answer YES when the subject has no code field.

rules.guidance: Credential Manager is the recommended Jetpack API for credential exchange in Android apps.
rules.check: If the screen signs the user in or up, does it offer Credential Manager (passkeys, saved passwords, Sign in with Google through CredentialManager.getCredential) rather than only a hand-built username-and-password form? Judge from the source. Answer YES when the screen does not sign anyone in.

rules.guidance: FLAG_SECURE is a Window flag that tells Android not to allow screenshots or to display the window view on a non-secure display (such as Casting the screen). This is useful for applications that need to protect sensitive information, like banking apps or password managers.
rules.check: Does the picture avoid showing a secret in full and in plain text — a whole payment card number, a password, a private key or recovery code — showing it masked or shortened (for example only a card's last four digits) unless the user has just asked to reveal it? Answer YES when nothing secret is shown.

rules.guidance: Wear OS users can choose between various input options from Remote Input. … RemoteInput and Wear OS apps expect only single-line text entry.
rules.check: Does the screen take any text through the system's remote input — RemoteInput launched with androidx.wear.input's RemoteInputIntentHelper, which offers dictation, emoji, canned and smart replies and the keyboard — or through speech recognition (RecognizerIntent), rather than drawing its own on-screen keyboard or editable multi-line text fields on the watch? Answer YES when the screen takes no text, or when its text entry is a button or chip that opens remote input.

rules.guidance: Help people complete tasks on the watch within seconds to avoid ergonomic discomfort or arm fatigue. … Support speech-to-text, because it's much faster on a watch.
rules.check: Does the screen keep typed input to a single short entry, offering choices, voice, or continuing on the phone (RemoteActivityHelper from androidx.wear:wear-remote-interactions) for anything longer, rather than a form of several text fields to fill in on the watch? Answer YES when the screen asks for no more than one short text entry.

rules.guidance: Credential Manager is the recommended API for authentication on Wear OS. … There are two other acceptable authentication methods for Wear OS apps: OAuth 2.0 (either variant), and Mobile Auth Token Data Layer Sharing.
rules.check: If the screen signs the user in, does it use the Wear OS methods — Credential Manager (passkeys first, through CredentialManager.getCredential), OAuth 2.0 (PKCE with RemoteAuthClient, or the Device Authorization Grant opening the verification page on the phone with RemoteActivityHelper), or a token the phone app shares over the Data Layer — or Horologist's auth-composables-material3 screens built on them, rather than a hand-built username and password form typed on the watch? Judge from the source and the screen. Answer YES when the screen does not sign anyone in.

rules.guidance: Offer at least one secondary option to handle users dismissing Credential Manager. Provide at least two distinct sign-in options in total.
rules.check: If the screen is where the user chooses how to sign in, does it offer at least two distinct ways (for example Credential Manager and an OAuth or phone hand-off option), rather than a single one such as only "Sign in on phone"? Answer YES when the screen is not a sign-in choice.

rules.guidance: Don't require authentication for all functionality. Instead, provide as many features as possible to the user without requiring them to sign in.
rules.check: If the screen asks the user to sign in, is that tied to an action that needs an account, or does it offer a way to skip or continue as a guest, rather than a sign-in wall in front of everything? Answer YES when the screen does not ask the user to sign in.

rules.guidance: It's also common for a text field to have a corresponding descriptive label that describes what users must enter as input.
rules.check: Does every text field have a visible label — the field's label, or text beside it — saying what to enter, rather than placeholder (hint) text alone, which disappears once typing starts? Answer YES when the subject has no text field.

rules.guidance: When defining error states, you can inform the accessibility services of its error semantics, and provide expanded error messaging.
rules.check: Where a field is shown in an error state, is it marked as an error (isError = true, or semantics { error(…) }) with the message in its supporting text or error semantics, so it is announced, rather than only turning red? Answer YES when nothing is in an error state.

rules.guidance: TextField lets you set keyboard configuration options, such as the keyboard layout, or enable the autocorrect if it's supported by the keyboard.
rules.check: Judge from the source. Do the text fields' KeyboardOptions fit what each takes — keyboardType Email for an email address, Number or Phone for digits, Password for a password — with an imeAction that moves on (Next) between fields and finishes (Done, Go, Search or Send) on the last? Answer YES when the subject has no text field, or only free text where the defaults fit.

rules.guidance: For each UI element in your app, include a description that describes the element's purpose. In most cases, you include this description in the element's contentDescription attribute
rules.check: Does every control that shows only an icon — an icon button, a floating action button without text, an icon-only toggle or chip — carry a content description naming its action (its accessibility node has a label)? Controls with visible text need none. Answer YES when there are no icon-only controls.

rules.guidance: If a UI element has a contentDescription parameter but is purely decorative (such as an Icon that is part of another UI element), pass null to avoid redundant labeling.
rules.check: Are purely decorative images and icons — ones beside text that already says the same, or inside a control that is already labelled — given no content description (contentDescription = null), so a screen reader does not read the same thing twice? Answer YES when there are none.

rules.guidance: When building a custom component, make sure you provide all relevant semantic properties for accessibility purposes. For example, if your component mimics a standard control like a switch or button, these properties include the component's role (such as Role.Switch or Role.Button), stateDescription (such as "On", "Off", "Checked", or "Not checked"), and any relevant action labels.
rules.check: Does every on/off, checked or selected control (switch, checkbox, radio button, toggle button, selectable chip or row) expose its state — a standard toggle component, Modifier.toggleable / selectable, or a stateDescription — rather than a plain clickable whose state shows only visually? The accessibility nodes' states (checked, selected) show it. Answer YES when there are no such controls.

rules.guidance: If a particular element represents a heading, you can indicate its purpose for accessibility services by setting the heading property in the semantics modifier.
rules.check: Where the screen has section titles (text heading a group of items), are they marked as headings (semantics { heading() }, or a component that does so) so screen-reader users can move between sections? Answer YES when there are no section titles.

rules.guidance: Use the parent container's semantics modifier to set mergeDescendants to true. … When grouping related elements like in the previous example, make only the parent container interactive. Avoid adding clickable or focusable modifiers to the inner child elements.
rules.check: Is each list row, card or tile that reads as one item a single focus stop — one clickable (or mergeDescendants) parent whose icon, title and subtitle belong to that one accessibility node — with separate focus stops only for distinct secondary actions? Answer YES when there are no such items.

rules.guidance: To assist users with color vision deficiencies, use cues other than color to distinguish UI elements within your app's screens.
rules.check: Is every meaning carried by colour also carried by something else — an icon, text, a shape, an outline or an underline? An error shown only in red, a selected item only tinted or a link only coloured would not be. Answer YES when colour is only decorative.

rules.guidance: isTraversalGroup and traversalIndex are semantic properties that let you influence the traversal order for accessibility services in scenarios where Compose's default sorting algorithm is not sufficient.
rules.check: Would accessibility focus follow the visual reading order — in the accessibility nodes, top to bottom and start to end, with each group (a card, a pane, a floating button over a list) visited together — rather than jumping between unrelated regions? Answer YES when the nodes' order matches the layout.

rules.guidance: If the text is smaller than 18sp, or if the text is bold and smaller than 14sp, use foreground and background colors that result in a color contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. For all other text, set the color contrast ratio to at least 3:1.
rules.check: Where the subject's measured accessibility checks include a contrast result, decide from that; otherwise judge the picture. Does all text meet 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for text 18sp and larger, or bold and 14sp or larger)? Disabled controls are exempt.

rules.guidance: you should still perform UI testing with the maximum font size enabled (200%) to ensure that your app applies the font sizes correctly and can accommodate larger font sizes without impacting usability.
rules.check: Is the essential text — titles, action labels, values, error messages — shown in full rather than cut off, ellipsized mid-phrase or clipped by its container? Content cut at a scrollable edge where more can be scrolled to is not truncation; content cut at the very end of a scroll is. Until a large-font render is attached, judge the picture at its own scale, and from the source note fixed heights or maxLines = 1 on essential text.

rules.guidance: To allow users to adjust the font size, specify font size in scalable pixels (sp)
rules.check: Are text sizes given in sp (the theme's typography, or .sp) rather than dp or pixels, and do containers holding text avoid fixed heights that would clip it as the font scale grows? A large-font render is not attached yet, so decide from the source; if the source is not given, ask for it rather than guessing. Answer YES when the source sets no text size or container height.

rules.guidance: Use the stringResource API to retrieve a string statically defined in XML resources.
rules.check: Judge from the source. Is the screen's user-visible text read from string resources (stringResource(R.string.…)) or passed in by the caller, rather than written as literals inside the screen's composables? Sample content a @Preview function passes in is data, not hard-coding. Answer YES when the source shows no user-visible literal in the screen itself.

rules.guidance: People who use RTL scripts prefer an RTL user interface, which includes right-aligned menus, right-aligned text, and forward arrows pointing to the left.
rules.check: Are directional icons (back and forward arrows, chevrons, send, undo and redo) the auto-mirrored variants (Icons.AutoMirrored.…, or a drawable with android:autoMirrored="true"), so they point the right way in a right-to-left layout? A right-to-left render is not attached yet, so decide from the source; if the source is not given, ask for it rather than guessing. Answer YES when there are no directional icons.

rules.guidance: Warning: Prefer colors from the theme rather than hard-coded colors. Even though it's possible to access colors using the colorResource function, it's recommended that the colors of your app are defined in a MaterialTheme
rules.check: Judge from the source. Do the subject's colours come from the theme (MaterialTheme.colorScheme roles, or the component's defaults) rather than hard-coded Color(0x…) or Color.Red literals? Images and brand artwork are exempt. Answer YES when the source sets no colour.

rules.guidance: To support light and dark themes, use isSystemInDarkTheme().
rules.check: Does the theme follow the system setting to a dark colour scheme (isSystemInDarkTheme(), or dynamic colour for both), rather than a light scheme only? When a dark render is attached, judge it: is everything still legible, with nothing light-on-light or dark-on-dark? Answer YES for a subject that only uses the theme it is given.

rules.guidance: High-emphasis buttons. These are for primary actions in an application, such as "submit" and "save."
rules.check: Does the screen give high emphasis (a filled button or an extended floating action button) to at most one action, its primary one, with the others in lower-emphasis styles (tonal, outlined or text buttons)? Answer YES when at most one high-emphasis action is visible.

rules.guidance: Confirming user action, such as when deleting a file.
rules.check: Where the screen offers a destructive or irreversible action (delete, remove, discard), is it confirmed (a confirmation dialog) or undoable (a snackbar with Undo), and not styled as the screen's primary filled action? Judge from the source where it shows the click handler. Answer YES when there is no such action.

rules.guidance: Progress indicators visually surface the status of an operation. They use motion to bring to the user's attention how near completion the process is, such as loading or processing data.
rules.check: Judge from the source. Where the screen shows content that loads (from a repository, the network or a state holder), does it handle the loading state (a progress indicator) and a failure (a message, with a way to retry), rather than drawing only the loaded content? A preview of one state is fine when the source shows the others are handled. Answer YES when the content is static.
